paragraphs.text: Lesson 11 at the post office and bank.
Welcome to lesson 11 of the everyday English speaking course.
Today we're going to run some errands.
Erands are activities of daily life that you do outside your house.
For example, going to the bank and going to the store.
First let's go to the post office.
That's the place where you can send mail and packages.
Conversation number 1 at the post office.
Good morning.
Good morning. I'd like to mail this package to Mexico.
Do you want to send it first class, priority or express?
What's the difference?
First class will get there in 15 to 18 business days, priority in 8 to 10 business days, and express in 2 to 3 business days.
First class is fine. It's not urgent. Can I get a tracking number for the package?
Sorry, only with express mail.
I'll stick with first class.
Would you like to add insurance or delivery confirmation?
No, that's okay.
I'll just need you to fill in this customs form.
Sure. How much does it cost to mail postcards?
$0.32 each.
Then I'd like to mail these 10 postcards too.
Alright, would you like to buy any stamps or envelopes today?
No thanks.
Okay, your total is $33.70.
Conversation, vocabulary and phrases.
The word mail can be a noun or a verb.
Mail as a noun refers to the letters and magazines you receive.
Mail as a verb means to send something through the post office system.
At the post office you'll probably have a choice of several sending options.
First class mail is the slowest and cheapest option.
Priority mail is a little faster and a little more expensive.
And express mail is the fastest, most expensive option.
Some post offices also offer overnight delivery, which means it's guaranteed to arrive the next day.
The post office attendant refers to business days.
Business days are Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, except for major national holidays.
A tracking number is a number that identifies the location of the package.
You can put the tracking number into the post office website to find out where the package is,
or if it has already been delivered.
You can also get insurance.
This means you would receive money as compensation if your package got lost or destroyed in the mail.
Or delivery confirmation.
That's a service that notifies you when the package is delivered.
Finally, you can also buy stamps and envelopes at the post office.
An envelope is what you put a letter into in order to mail it.
And a stamp is the evidence that you've paid to send the letter.
Notice the attendance pronunciation in the question starting with, would you like?
It sounds like, would you like?
Would you like to buy any stamps or envelopes today?
Would you like to add insurance or delivery confirmation?
Let's practice and review the post office phrases.
I'd like to mail or send this package.
I'd like to mail or send some letters.
I'd like to mail or send some postcards.
I'd like to buy some stamps or envelopes.
I'd like to add insurance or delivery confirmation.
I'd like to send it overnight. It's urgent.
Can I get a tracking number for the package?
When will it arrive?
Conversation number two at the bank.
Before we go to the bank, let's learn some money vocabulary.
As in most countries, the United States has two types of money.
Paper money called bills.
And metal money called coins.
Don't confuse coins with cash.
Cash includes both bills and coins.
It is used to distinguish paying with physical money from paying with a credit card or check.
The diagram in the lesson text will help.
In the US, the different coins have different names.
The one cent coin is called a penny.
The five cent coin is called a nickel.
The ten cent coin is called a dime.
The twenty-five cent coin is called a quarter.
There is also a fifty cent coin called a half dollar, but it's not very common.
Canada, Australia and New Zealand also use the system of dollars and cents.
In the United Kingdom, however, the unit of currency is the pound,
and each pound is made of one hundred pence.
If you're visiting an English-speaking country, you'll probably want to change money, or exchange money,
from one currency into another.
Let's listen to an example conversation about changing money at the bank.
The person who works with customers at the bank is called a bank teller.
Hi, what can I do for you today?
I'd like to change some money. Could you tell me the exchange rate for euros to dollars?
One euro is worth a dollar and twenty-five cents, and there's also an exchange fee of two percent.
Here's three hundred euros.
That'll be three hundred and seventy-five dollars, minus the fee gives a total of three sixty-seven fifty.
Would you like that in large or small bills?
Small bills, please.
Okay, here's two hundred dollars and twenty's, one hundred and fifty dollars and ten's,
seventeen dollars and fives and ones, and fifty cents.
Thanks.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
The exchange rate tells you how to convert from one country's currency to another,
for example, one euro to one dollar and twenty-five cents,
or one dollar to four point five Argentine pesos.
The expression, could you tell me, is a polite way to ask for information?
It is more indirect and more polite than saying just tell me or I want to know.
Also, in this conversation, as well as in the post office dialogue, the man uses the phrase,
I'd like to, instead of I want to, again because it is more polite.
The teller may ask if you want your money in large or small bills.
Large bills would be fifty dollar or one hundred dollar bills,
and small bills would be twenty's, ten's, fives and ones.
In addition to exchanging money, here are a few more things you can do at the bank.
I'd like to open a checking account.
I'd like to open a checking, savings or investment account.
A checking account is for day-to-day expenses.
A savings account is for keeping money for a long time.
And an investment account is for putting money into the stock market.
I'd like to make a deposit.
Or I'd like to make a withdrawal.
Make a deposit means put money into the account.
And make a withdrawal means to take money out of the account.
I'd like to deposit a check.
That means put the money from a check into the account.
I'd like to cash a check.
Cash a check means exchange a check for money.
I'd like to take out a loan.
Take out a loan means borrow money from the bank to pay back later.
I'd like to check my balance.
That means find out how much money you currently have in your account.
I'd like to talk to a manager about a problem with my account.
If you want to find a machine to withdraw, take out money, you can ask somebody.
Is there an ATM around here?
Or where's the nearest ATM?
Another question you might want to ask an employee of the bank is,
does this ATM accept international cards?
Now try the quiz to test your vocabulary from the banking and post office phrases.
